stats-water-potential-s1.title: Potato cores in sucrose solutions
stats-water-potential-s1.text: Students weighed cores cut from one potato, left five cores in each of six sucrose solutions in open beakers at 22 °C for 24 hours, and weighed them again. The graph shows the mean percent change in mass; error bars show 95% confidence intervals.

stats-water-potential-s2.title: Three solutions at 25 °C
stats-water-potential-s2.text: A teacher prepared three solutions in open beakers at 25 °C. Use R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K) and T = 298 K.

items.q: Estimate the sucrose concentration at which the potato cores would neither gain nor lose mass. Give your answer in mol/L to two decimal places.

why.correct: The line crosses 0% between 0.2 M (+5%) and 0.4 M (−5%). Zero is halfway along that segment: 0.2 + 0.2 × (5 ÷ 10) = 0.30 mol/L.

items.q: Calculate the solute potential of a 0.30 mol/L sucrose solution at 22 °C. Give your answer in bars to one decimal place.

why.correct: Ψs = −iCRT = −(1)(0.30 mol/L)(0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K))(295 K) = −7.35, about −7.4 bars. Sucrose does not ionize, so i = 1; T = 22 + 273 = 295 K.

items.q: What does the concentration where the cores neither gain nor lose mass tell you?
options: At that concentration the solution's water potential equals the potato cells' water potential, so there is no net water movement.
At that concentration the potato cells contain exactly 0.30 mol/L of sucrose, the same as the surrounding solution in the beaker.
At that concentration water stops crossing the membranes in either direction, because the aquaporins close.
At that concentration the cores are plasmolyzed, so they can no longer take in or lose water by osmosis.

why.correct: No net mass change means no net water movement, which happens when Ψ outside equals Ψ inside. So the cells' water potential is about −7.4 bars. Water still crosses both ways; the flows just balance.
options: Correct: equal water potentials, no net flow.
Cell water potential depends on all its solutes and its pressure potential, not only on sucrose.
Water keeps crossing in both directions at equal rates; the balance is dynamic.
Plasmolysis happens in solutions much more concentrated than this, where cells lose a lot of water.

items.q: Why did the cores in 0.8 mol/L sucrose lose mass?
options: The solution had a lower (more negative) water potential than the cells, so water moved out of the cells by osmosis.
Sucrose moved into the cells by diffusion and pushed water out, so the cores became lighter as a result.
The solution had a higher water potential than the cells, so water moved from the solution into the cells.
The high sucrose concentration dissolved part of the potato cell walls, so the cores lost solid mass.

why.correct: 0.8 M sucrose at 295 K has Ψ = −(1)(0.8)(0.0831)(295) ≈ −19.6 bars, far below the cells' ≈ −7.4 bars. Water moves from higher to lower Ψ, out of the cells.
options: Correct.
Sucrose moving in would add mass; the loss is water leaving.
If the solution's Ψ were higher, water would move in and the cores would gain mass.
Sucrose does not dissolve cell walls; the change is water.

items.q: Why did the students record percent change in mass rather than change in grams?
options: The cores did not all start at the same mass, and percent change lets cores of different sizes be compared fairly.
Percent change turns losses into positive numbers, which makes a graph of the results easier to read and compare.
Change in grams would be the same for each core, so it would not show any effect of sucrose concentration.
The balance could weigh just in percent, so grams were converted to percent for the final report.

why.correct: A larger core gains or loses more grams in the same solution. Dividing by the starting mass removes that effect.
options: Correct.
Percent change can be negative, and it is here.
Grams lost or gained differ between cores, partly because of their different sizes; that is the problem percent change solves.
Balances read mass in grams; the percentage is calculated from them.

items.q: Calculate the solute potential of the 0.1 mol/L NaCl solution at 25 °C. Give your answer in bars to two decimal places.

why.correct: Ψs = −iCRT = −(2)(0.1)(0.0831)(298) = −4.95 bars. NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so i = 2.

items.q: Why does the CaCl₂ solution have three times the solute potential magnitude of the sucrose solution at the same molar concentration?
options: Each CaCl₂ unit dissolves into three particles (Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻), and solute potential depends on the number of dissolved particles.
CaCl₂ molecules are about three times heavier than sucrose molecules, so each one lowers the water potential of the solution three times as much.
Calcium ions carry a charge of 2+, and solute potential depends on the charge on each dissolved particle.
CaCl₂ binds three times as many water molecules into covalent bonds, removing them from the solution.

why.correct: Solute potential depends on the concentration of dissolved particles. Sucrose stays as one particle (i = 1); CaCl₂ gives three ions (i = 3).
options: Correct: particle count, captured by i.
Mass is not in −iCRT; sucrose molecules are actually heavier than CaCl₂ units.
Charge is not what i counts; i counts particles.
Ions attract water by hydrogen bonding and charge attraction, not covalent bonds.

items.q: A bag made of membrane that lets water through but not sucrose or ions is filled with the 0.1 mol/L sucrose solution and placed in a beaker of the 0.1 mol/L NaCl solution. What happens?
options: Water leaves the bag, because the NaCl solution's water potential (−4.95 bars) is lower than the sucrose solution's (−2.48 bars).
Water enters the bag, because sucrose molecules are larger than ions and attract more water molecules to them.
Nothing happens, because the two solutions have the same molar concentration of solute, 0.1 mol/L each, on both sides of the bag.
Sodium and chloride ions enter the bag until both sides have equal numbers of dissolved particles.

why.correct: Equal molarity is not equal water potential. NaCl gives twice as many particles, so its Ψ is lower, and water moves from the bag (−2.48 bars) to the beaker (−4.95 bars).
options: Correct.
Particle number, not particle size, sets solute potential.
Same molarity, different i: the NaCl solution has twice as many particles.
The membrane in the question lets water through but not ions.

items.q: Select ALL solutions that would have the same water potential as the 0.1 mol/L NaCl solution at 25 °C in an open beaker.
options: 0.2 mol/L sucrose
0.1 mol/L glucose
0.05 mol/L NaCl
0.2 mol/L CaCl₂
0.3 mol/L sucrose

why.correct: Water potential depends on i × C. NaCl at 0.1 M gives iC = 0.2. Only 0.2 M sucrose matches (1 × 0.2).
options: Different: 1 × 0.1 = 0.1, half as many particles.
Different: 2 × 0.05 = 0.1.
Different: 3 × 0.2 = 0.6.
Different: 1 × 0.3 = 0.3.

items.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of −9.0 bars and a pressure potential of +3.0 bars. Calculate its water potential in bars, to one decimal place.
The cell from the previous question (Ψ = −6.0 bars) is placed in a large beaker of 0.3 mol/L sucrose at 22 °C (Ψ ≈ −7.4 bars). What happens to the cell?
options: It loses water, so its pressure potential falls as its turgor drops.
It gains water, so its pressure potential rises as it becomes more turgid.
It neither gains nor loses water, because its solute potential is more negative than the solution's.
It gains sucrose, so its solute potential becomes less negative over time.

why.correct: Water moves from higher Ψ (−6.0, the cell) to lower Ψ (−7.4, the solution). As water leaves, the cell pushes less on its wall, so ΨP falls (and Ψs becomes a little more negative) until the cell's Ψ matches −7.4 bars.
options: Correct.
Water moves toward the lower water potential, which is the solution here.
Movement depends on total Ψ, not on Ψs alone; the cell's Ψ (−6.0) is higher than the solution's.
The question concerns water; sucrose movement is not what sets the direction here.

items.q: Calculate the solute potential of a 0.5 mol/L sucrose solution at 27 °C. Give your answer in bars to one decimal place.
A student calculates the solute potential of 0.30 mol/L sucrose at 22 °C but uses T = 22 instead of 295. How does her answer compare with the correct value?
options: It is about 13 times too close to zero (−0.55 instead of −7.4 bars).
It is about 13 times too negative (−98 instead of −7.4 bars).
It is the same, because temperature units cancel in the equation.
It has the wrong sign, because Celsius temperatures can be negative.

why.correct: −(1)(0.30)(0.0831)(22) = −0.55 bars, while 295 K gives −7.35 bars: 295 ÷ 22 ≈ 13 times smaller in size. R is defined per kelvin, so T must be in kelvin.
options: Correct.
Using a smaller T makes the magnitude smaller, not larger.
R has units L·bar/(mol·K); the K only cancels if T is in kelvin.
22 °C is positive, so the sign is unchanged; the size is wrong.

items.q: A solution has a water potential of −7.4 bars. What is this in megapascals (MPa)?
options: −74 MPa
−7.4 MPa
Correct.
This multiplies by 10; bars are the smaller unit, so the MPa number is smaller.
Bars and MPa are different units.
This divides by 100; the factor is 10.

items.q: For a solution in an open beaker, why is its water potential equal to its solute potential?
options: An open beaker puts no extra pressure on the solution, so its pressure potential is 0.
An open beaker lets solutes evaporate, so the solute potential becomes the one potential left.
In an open beaker the solute potential is 0, so the pressure potential is what counts.
Water potential is defined as solute potential whenever the temperature is held constant.

why.correct: Ψ = ΨP + Ψs. Exposed to the atmosphere with no wall pushing back, ΨP = 0, so Ψ = Ψs.
options: Correct.
Dissolved solutes such as sucrose do not evaporate.
Any dissolved solute makes Ψs negative; it is ΨP that is 0.
Pressure, not temperature, decides whether ΨP is 0.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the water potential of a solution in an open beaker in order.
options: Find i (1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl) and C in mol/L.
Convert the temperature to kelvin: °C + 273.
Calculate Ψs = −iCRT with R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K).
Add ΨP, which is 0 for an open container, to get Ψ.
Compare Ψ values: water moves toward the more negative one.

why.correct: Gather i and C, convert T, calculate Ψs, add ΨP, then compare.
